WhatsApp appointment reminders for a clinic: case study

A system that every evening messages patients who have an appointment the next day on WhatsApp and lets them confirm, reschedule or request an appointment with buttons.

  • Problem. When a patient forgets an appointment, the clinic loses that slot and the front desk spends time confirming one by one.
  • What I did. I designed and built appointment reminders and booking requests over WhatsApp with Make and Google Sheets, and proposed them to a clinic.
  • What I found. I reviewed every message and found 4 errors that would have reached the patient.

Status. Tested with Meta's test number and my phone. Pilot with the clinic: in progress. There are no metrics yet. The names, phone numbers and appointments in the images and messages are illustrative, not real. I do not publish the clinic's name or prices.

Role
Conversation design, automation build, documentation and commercial proposal
Tools
WhatsApp Business Platform (Meta), Make, Google Sheets
Scope
Daily reminder with buttons, menu, appointment request, rescheduling, follow-up, opt-out and front-desk alert
Out of scope
Real-time availability scheduling, an AI assistant and medical software integration (quoted separately)

Problem and goal

The problem. When a patient forgets an appointment, the clinic loses that slot and its revenue. The front desk also spends time every day calling or messaging people one by one to confirm. With 20 appointments a day and 2 minutes per confirmation, that is about 40 minutes a day, close to 3 hours a week (an example calculation from the proposal, not a measurement from the clinic).

The goal. The schedule alerts patients on its own, they reply with one tap, and the front desk can focus on the people in the clinic. The system does not replace the front desk: it removes the repetitive work and always leaves a way to reach a person.

How it works

There are two flows. The first runs once a day; the second answers when the patient writes.

Reminders. Every evening the system looks in the schedule for next-day appointments with no reminder sent and no opt-out, sends a Meta-approved template (a text Meta reviews before a business can use it to message someone first) with name, date, time and doctor, and marks in the schedule that it already sent it so the message is not repeated.

Replies. The patient taps Confirm or Reschedule, or writes to the clinic and gets a menu with three buttons: request an appointment, hours and location, and front desk. To request an appointment they pick a service, a day and a time of day with lists and buttons. The request is saved in the sheet and the front desk confirms it, because the system does not reserve slots by itself yet.

This is how it looks in the patient's chat, with fictional data. The texts were written in Spanish and are translated here, and the opt-out text is illustrative:

Transcript of three messages from the example, translated from Spanish (the names are illustrative, not real):

Reminder. "Hi, Ana. A reminder of your appointment at [Clinic] tomorrow, Saturday, October 17, at 4:00 p.m. with Dr. Luis Elizondo. Can you confirm you will attend?" Buttons: Confirm and Reschedule.

Reschedule. "No problem, Sofía. We let the front desk know you need to change your appointment. Which day suits you better?" Button: See dates.

No history. "We found no previous appointments with this number. Is this your first visit?" Buttons: Yes, first visit and I am already a patient.

Privacy. The message only carries name, date, time and doctor, never the reason for the visit, and the sheet the automation reads has no diagnosis columns. It only messages people who gave consent, and anyone who writes BAJA (opt out) stops receiving messages. Because this is health data in Mexico, the clinic must have a privacy notice and the patients' consent. This does not claim legal compliance: it is what has to exist before starting.

Iterating on the conversational content

Once the system worked, I reviewed every message by putting myself in the patient's place, from start to finish. It was my own heuristic review, with no testing with patients. I found four problems that could cause real mistakes and several of tone and clarity. I fixed them and tested them with real messages to my own phone. The messages themselves are in Spanish; I translate them here.

Message Before After Why
Reschedule from the reminder "We cancelled your appointment tomorrow" "No problem, Sofía. We let the front desk know you need to change your appointment. Which day suits you better?" The text said "cancelled" when the patient asked to reschedule, and the schedule said something else. Now the date list arrives in the same message
Follow-up with history "Your last appointment was 10/16/2026", although that appointment was the next day "Your last appointment was on Saturday, October 17. Since your follow-up is every 2 weeks, your next one is Saturday, October 31. Choose that date or another nearby one." Button: "See dates" It takes the most recent past appointment and shows it with its weekday. A wrong fact in a health message erodes trust in the whole system
Follow-up without history No message was sent "We found no previous appointments with this number. Is this your first visit?" Buttons: "Yes, first visit" and "I am already a patient" Silence reads as a failure. Every path must end in a reply and a way out
Date list 16/10/2026, 17/10/2026… "Friday, Oct. 16" People think "on Friday", not in numeric dates. The list leaves out Sundays and days without consultations, because offering closed days creates impossible requests
Main menu "Type 1 to book or 2 to talk to the front desk" Buttons: "Request appointment", "Hours and location" and "Front desk" It was the only step that required typing. I added the most frequent question
Talk to the front desk "Someone from the front desk will be with you in a moment" "We let the front desk know. They will contact you here during opening hours." "In a moment" is a promise that is not kept at night
Patient name The WhatsApp profile name "Hi, Sofía." The name comes from the schedule, not the profile. A relative can book from their number, and a profile name can be a nickname

Accessibility review

In a second round I checked how each message sounds with a screen reader, how an older person reads it, and how clear it is without relying on emojis. The clinic is in Mexico, so the 12-hour clock and Spanish date formats below refer to Spanish-language messages.

  • Dates. In lists, "Viernes 16 de oct." instead of "Vie 16/10", which the reader pronounced as "sixteen slash ten". In messages, the full month, because there is no character limit there.
  • Times. 12-hour format ("4:00 p.m."), which is how most people in Mexico say the time, especially older people.
  • Confirmations. With labels and a final period (Day, Time, Doctor) so the reader pauses.
  • Emojis. Each one sits next to a word that says the same thing. I removed the arrow emojis from the Follow-up dates, which the reader announced as "back button".
  • Time-of-day buttons. Just "Morning" and "Afternoon", with the ranges written in the message.
  • Appointment request. The message says it is a request and not yet a confirmed appointment, so nobody shows up to an appointment that does not exist.

Design decisions

  • Lists and buttons instead of forms. WhatsApp's native form (Flows, a form that opens inside the chat) was blocked by Meta on the test account. Lists and buttons give a similar experience and work on any account.
  • Every reply carries its context. Each option's identifier (an internal code that travels with every button or list item) stores what the patient already chose, so the system does not need to remember the conversation or ask again.
  • Ask for the minimum. Phone and name arrive with the message; the front desk fills in the rest when confirming.
  • Always a way to a person. Every path offers talking to the front desk.
  • Informal "you" (tuteo). I considered switching to the formal register for older patients and kept the informal one throughout the flow. Changing it would mean a new template approved by Meta.

Proposal and documentation

I prepared the pilot proposal for the clinic and three documents so the work can be repeated with another client:

  1. Client requirements. A list of what the clinic must have before starting: a responsible person, accounts, a phone number, business details, payment, patient consent and schedule.
  2. Implementation checklist. Ordered steps in 15 phases, with a table of known errors and their fixes, built from the failures I ran into while building it.
  3. How to explain it to the client. A plain-language guide: what they gain, what they provide and what each part costs, and what not to promise, such as a percentage reduction in no-shows or a start date before Meta's approvals.

The proposal separates what is included from what is quoted separately and sets out a three-month pilot in which the clinic shares metrics at 30 and 90 days.

What I will measure in the pilot

These metrics will be measured at 30 and 90 days into the pilot. There is no data for any of them yet.

  • Confirmation rate. How many patients answer Confirm or Reschedule to the reminder.
  • No-shows. Compared with the last month before the pilot.
  • Front-desk minutes saved. The proposal's 40 minutes a day is an example, not a measurement; the pilot will replace it with real time.

What I learned

  • Reviewing with the system running. Reviewing every message end to end turned up real errors: a "cancelled" when the patient asked to reschedule, dates without a weekday, a future date shown as past, and an empty reply for someone with no history.
  • Every path needs a reply and a way out. Silence reads as a failure, so every path ends in a message and the option to talk to the front desk.
  • Depending on Meta limits the options. The native form (Flows) was not available on the test account, so I used lists and buttons, which work on any account.
  • The tone has a cost to change. I kept the informal register, and moving to the formal one later would mean a new template approved by Meta.
